fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk calls Kentucky bluegrass the most widely used lawn grass in Colorado, tells anyone choosing a grass to ask whether the site is sunny or shady and whether tree growth will later make it shadier, and says no grass species is perfect for all situations and uses.
quote: Is the lawn site sunny or shady? If sunny, will tree growth later make the area more shady? … Kentucky bluegrass is a good choice for many situations and uses. It’s the most widely used lawn grass in Colorado. … No grass species is perfect for all situations and uses. Selecting the proper grass for the lawn’s intended use and for the site is the first step toward creating a quality lawn.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1521, Choosing a Lawn Grass in Colorado
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. The page does not itself rate bluegrass's shade tolerance; that is GardenNotes #561 (gn561-shade-by-species).

fact: CSU Extension's turfgrass selection guide rates Kentucky bluegrass's shade tolerance poor to fair but credits its wear tolerance and recovery, says turf-type tall fescue does well in shade and is wear tolerant, gives the fine fescues very good shade tolerance but only moderate wear tolerance, says buffalograss needs at least a half day of full sun and won't take heavy, constant traffic, and calls blue grama neither shade nor traffic tolerant.
quote: Kentucky bluegrass, Poa pratensis, has been a standard for the beautiful green lawn since the days of King Louis of France due to its dense stand, rich bluish green color, and wear tolerance. … High recuperative potential and rate … Poor to fair shade tolerance … Turf-Type Tall Fescue (Festuca arundinacea) … Wear-tolerant … Does well in shade … Buffalograss (Buchloë dactyloides) … Excellent heat and drought resistance … Poor to fair shade tolerance. Needs at least a half day of full sun. … Will not tolerate heavy, constant traffic. … Fine Fescues (Festuca spp.) … Very good shade tolerance … Moderate wear tolerance (NOT for high traffic areas) … Slow to recuperate from traffic injury … Blue Grama (Bouteloua gracilis) … Excellent cold, heat, drought tolerance … Not traffic tolerant … Not shade tolerant
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #561, Turfgrass Species Selection Guidelines (Tony Koski; revised January 2012)
notes: Read from the PDF (pdftotext) on 2026-09-25. Bullet glyphs dropped; the … marks join lines from the advantages and disadvantages lists of each species. The 2025 fine fescue fact sheet (csu-fine-fescue-front-range) gives fine fescue 'good to very good' shade tolerance; the page uses that newer wording.

fact: CSU Extension's fine fescue fact sheet gives the fine fescues good to very good shade tolerance and moderate wear tolerance, calls hard fescue especially well suited to the Front Range for its heat tolerance, says constant root-zone moisture makes fine fescue decline and thin, and says it still needs 18 to 20 inches of supplemental irrigation in a normal Front Range year, against 24 inches for bluegrass.
quote: Good to very good shade tolerance … Moderate wear tolerance (not for constant high traffic areas) … Slower to recuperate from traffic injury … Hard fescue (Festuca longifolia or duriuscula) is gaining wider use due to its better heat tolerance, relative to the other fine fescues. Its tolerance to warm summer conditions makes it especially well-suited to use in the Front Range of Colorado. … The fine fescues prefer drier soils. Constant root zone moisture will cause rapid decline and thinning, as well as increase the potential for disease. While preferring dry soil, fine fescue lawns REQUIRE supplemental irrigation in Colorado. Fine fescue will require 18-20 inches of supplemental irrigation (compared to 24 inches for bluegrass) in a normal precipitation year (10-11 inches, April to October) along the Front Range.
source_label: CSU Extension, Fine Fescues for Lawns (Anthony Koski; reviewed July 2025)
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. The page footer says it references GardenNotes #564.

fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk says grass performs better in sun, that a lawn competing with a large tree for soil moisture may become overly dry while heavy watering in shade may aggravate lawn disease, and that in heavy shade ground covers or wood-chip mulch with shade-loving perennials may be more practical.
quote: Grass performs better in sunny locations. … Varieties of chewing fescue and creeping red fescue tolerate light shade quite well. Tall fescue has moderate shade tolerance and some varieties of Kentucky bluegrass have fair shade tolerance. … Heavy watering in shady areas may aggravate lawn disease problems. However, if the lawn has to compete with a large tree for soil moisture, the area may become overly dry. In heavy shade, it may be more practical to use ground covers or a wood-chip mulch with shade-loving perennials.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1518, Growing Grass in the Shade
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. Overlaps artificial-turf-vs-sod.csu-shade-grass; this record adds the tree-competition and watering sentences this page uses.

fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk defines full shade as the north or northeast side of buildings, walls or fences where the ground stays shaded all day in the growing season, medium shade as the shade of evergreens or dense trees such as maples or lindens, and light shade as a north-facing yard under open trees or spots with only morning sun, and says most shade in Colorado gardens is dry unless it gets runoff from rain or sprinklers.
quote: Full shade describes the lighting on the north or northeast side of buildings, walls or fences where, during the growing season, the ground remains in shade through the entire day. Medium or part shade is the shade cast by evergreens or dense, deciduous trees such as maples or lindens. … Light shade prevails in a north-facing yard under the canopies of ornamental or more open deciduous trees, and in the areas of the garden which usually receive only morning sun. … Most shade in Colorado gardens is dry shade, meaning that without watering, the soil is generally dry. However, if a shaded area receives runoff from rain or sprinklers, it may qualify as moist shade.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1127, Kinds of Shade
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25.

fact: CSU Extension's Master Gardener notes say southern exposures absorb more solar radiation than northern ones, and that a north-facing exposure will typically be cooler and moist while a south-facing one is hot and dry.
quote: Exposure – Southern exposures absorb more solar radiation than northern exposures. … Figure 2. Temperatures and growing season vary greatly based on exposure. A north facing exposure will typically be cooler and moist. A south facing exposure will typically be hot and dry.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #143, Plant Growth Factors: Temperature (reviewed March 2023)
notes: Read from the PDF (pdftotext) on 2026-09-25. The quote joins the Exposure paragraph's first sentence and the Figure 2 caption.

fact: The National Park Service says that at Rocky Mountain National Park's latitude, about 40.3 degrees north, the noon sun on the winter solstice is only about 26.2 degrees above the horizon.
quote: Also because of the earth's tilted orbit, the winter solstice marks the time when the sun is lowest in the sky in the Northern Hemisphere. At the latitude of the park (about 40.3 degrees north) the altitude of the sun at noon is only about 26.2 degrees above the horizon.
source_label: National Park Service, Rocky Mountain National Park, Winter Solstice (last updated March 31, 2012)
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. NoCo's towns sit at about 40.1 to 40.7 degrees north (territory.mjs Census points), so the park's figure is close for all of them (INFERENCE). The page's 'about twice as long' shadow is our arithmetic: 1 / tan(26.2 degrees) = 2.03.

fact: In a Colorado Front Range foothills catchment, USGS-led researchers found that north-facing slopes develop a seasonal snowpack while south-facing slopes get snow that comes and goes through winter and spring, and that south-facing soils are drier overall.
quote: Snowpack dynamics are strongly affected by aspect: Lodgepole pine forested north‐facing slopes develop a seasonal snowpack, whereas Ponderosa pine‐dotted south‐facing slopes experience intermittent snow accumulation throughout winter and spring. … south‐facing slope soils experience brief periods of rapid vertical transport following snowmelt events and are drier overall than north‐facing slopes.
source_label: Hinckley, Ebel, Barnes and others, Aspect control of water movement on hillslopes near the rain–snow transition of the Colorado Front Range, Hydrological Processes (published online October 17, 2012), abstract in the USGS Publications Warehouse
notes: Quote is from the abstract as printed on the USGS page (read 2026-09-25); the full paper was not read. The study site is a mountain catchment, not a Northern Colorado town; the page presents a north-side yard as the same effect at small scale, which is our reading. The site's county is a Denver-metro name the page must not print.

fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk says artificial turf collects leaves and wind-blown dirt and debris that must be removed, and that although it needs no mowing, fertilizing or watering and can be a legitimate solution for high-traffic sites, it lacks a living lawn's cooling effect and environmental benefits.
quote: Because it is not a living, transpiring plant, artificial turf does not provide the cooling effect of a living lawn and becomes quite warm on a sunny day. … artificial turf collects leaves and other wind-blown dirt and debris that must somehow be removed. … Although artificial turf does not require mowing, fertilizing, or watering and can be a legitimate solution for high traffic sites, it fails to provide the traditional landscape with the many environmental benefits of living grass.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1537, Artificial Turf for Lawns
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. The page also quotes a per-square-foot installation cost range; this record leaves it out and the guide prints no prices.

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's maintenance guidelines for infilled sports turf say leaves left on the surface migrate into the system, inhibiting drainage and compacting infill, that leafy trees should not stand next to a field if possible, and that moss, mold or algae may appear particularly where turf is in shade and damp.
quote: Remove airborne contaminants, such as leaves and other debris. If allowed to remain on the surface for any length of time, they will migrate into the system, inhibiting drainage and causing infill compaction. … Remove organic material, including animal waste, as soon as possible to impede the growth of algae, weed or moss growth. Leafy trees should not be located next to a field, if possible. … Moss, mold, or algae may appear in underutilized areas of the synthetic turf, particularly if it is in shade and damp.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)
notes: Read from the PDF (pdftotext) on 2026-09-25; 'caus-ing' is hyphenated across a line in the PDF. Written for sports fields; the page says so.

fact: TigerTurf, a turf maker, tells homeowners that damp conditions and rotting organic debris can foster algae in landscape turf, and to inspect for moss or algae especially in damp weather and in shaded areas.
quote: Damp conditions and rotting organic debris can foster the growth of algae in your landscape turf. You can prevent algae and moss taking hold in your lawn by following some simple steps: Regular inspection of your lawn for moss or algae, especially in damp weather and in shaded areas.
source_label: TigerTurf, Maintaining Your Synthetic Grass Lawn
notes: Read from the page HTML with curl on 2026-09-25. A turf maker's care page; it goes on to recommend its own treatment product, which the guide does not name.

fact: CSU Extension says feeding aphids excrete honeydew, a sticky waste that may cover leaves, branches, sidewalks and anything beneath an infested plant, that grayish sooty mold grows on it and it draws ants, yellowjackets, flies and bees, and it shows sooty mold on a walkway under a linden chronically infested with linden aphid.
quote: Feeding aphids excrete honeydew, a sticky fluid that can cause nuisance problems. … Honeydew is the waste material excreted by aphids and certain other phloem-sucking insects (e.g., soft scales, whiteflies, some leafhoppers). It may cover leaves, branches, sidewalks and anything that lies beneath an infested plant material. Grayish sooty mold grows on the honeydew, further detracting from plant appearance. Ants, yellowjacket wasps, flies, and bees are usually attracted to plants that are covered with honeydew. … Figure 4: Sooty mold growing on a wall and walkway underneath a linden tree that is chronically infested with linden aphid.
source_label: CSU Extension fact sheet 5.511, Aphids on Shade Trees and Ornamentals (W.S. Cranshaw; reviewed August 2025)
